items.stem: A Massachusetts prescriber telephones a retail pharmacy with a new EMERGENCY ORAL Schedule II order for a patient requiring immediate treatment. A certified technician answers, while a licensed pharmacist is on duty. The prescriber and the alleged emergency have not yet been verified. Who must assume responsibility for the oral emergency prescription record?

choices.text: The licensed pharmacist should communicate with the prescriber, establish the emergency and document the oral prescription.
choices.why: Correct. The pharmacist must reduce the emergency oral order to writing and follow federal emergency dispensing safeguards.

choices.text: The technician may accept and complete the legal oral order because national technician certification authorizes any new prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. For Schedule II emergency oral prescriptions, 21 CFR 1306.11(d) directs the pharmacist to reduce the order to writing and meet verification/follow-up conditions.

choices.text: A technician trainee may take the call if the pharmacist listens to a recording before dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.03(4)(c) expressly forbids technician trainees from taking telephone prescriptions.

choices.text: No oral record is needed if a replacement written order will be sent within seven days.
choices.why: Incorrect. The emergency oral order needs its own contemporaneous pharmacist record; follow-up is additional.

items.novelty_note: Emergency Schedule II is materially distinct from old oral Schedule VI receipt.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy cashier has no pharmacy technician license and works OUTSIDE the secured prescription area. Filled, pharmacist-verified, bagged prescriptions are ready for pickup. Which actions may the cashier perform as described? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Enter the prescription area alone to retrieve a loose Schedule VI stock bottle for a technician.
choices.why: Incorrect. Unlicensed cashiers may not handle unfilled prescription drugs or independently enter the secured prescription area.

choices.text: Take payment and hand over a verified bagged prescription after appropriate identity and pickup checks.
choices.why: Correct. Board Policy 2020-15 expressly permits unlicensed cashiers to sell filled, verified, bagged prescriptions.

choices.text: Select a new replacement drug and change the prescription directions when the pharmacist is busy.
choices.why: Incorrect. Clinical selection and prescription processing are not permitted unlicensed cashier activities.

choices.text: Extend the pharmacist's offer to counsel without personally giving clinical drug advice.
choices.why: Correct. The cashier may convey the offer but cannot provide clinical counseling.

items.novelty_note: Separates pickup logistics from prescription practice, unlike existing certified technician item.

items.stem: One Massachusetts pharmacist preceptor supervises FOUR licensed interns at a simulated medication-workflow workshop OUTSIDE any pharmacy. No real prescriptions or patient consultations occur. In the afternoon, all four will move into a hospital pharmacy and begin preparing actual patient prescriptions, still under that one preceptor. No waiver or second pharmacist applies. Which change is required?

choices.text: Nothing changes because four interns were permitted during the morning educational session.
choices.why: Incorrect. The educational four-intern exception does not carry into real prescription filling.

choices.text: Assign only Schedule VI prescriptions because the permitted intern count is determined by federal drug scheduling.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception depends on actual duties and patient-risk setting, not automatically on Schedule VI status.

choices.text: Restrict the real prescription-filling work to two interns per preceptor, or add another qualified preceptor.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.01(16) ordinarily limits direct supervision to two; Policy 2026-02 §II(A) excludes dispensing from its four-intern exception.

choices.text: Reclassify the four interns as technician trainees for the afternoon without separate licensure changes.
choices.why: Incorrect. A job-title change cannot evade the actual intern-supervision requirements.

items.novelty_note: A real-time shift from simulation to dispensing changes the applicable supervision cap.

items.stem: A Massachusetts COMMUNITY pharmacist has a valid physician CDTM agreement, written patient referral and consent for diabetes care, Massachusetts prescribing registration, and a personal DEA registration. The collaborating physician wants the pharmacist to begin prescribing Schedule IV alprazolam under the same community CDTM agreement. What is the legal result?

choices.text: It is allowed because a physician signature and DEA number authorize all Schedule III–V medicines.
choices.why: Incorrect. The community pharmacy CDTM rule directly prohibits Schedule II–V prescribing despite authorization language.

choices.text: A physician can allow it by reviewing the prescription within 24 hours of issuance.
choices.why: Incorrect. Communication within 24 hours does not waive an explicit controlled-schedule prohibition.

choices.text: Alprazolam automatically becomes Schedule VI when prescribed for a patient with diabetes.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient diagnosis does not change the drug's legal schedule.

choices.text: Community CDTM forbids prescribing Schedule II–V medicines, even with a personal DEA registration.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)3 excludes Schedules II–V from community pharmacist CDTM prescribing.

items.novelty_note: Distinguishes prescriber registration from restricted community CDTM scope.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist who neither compounds nor vaccinates reports precisely 20 CE hours in calendar year 2026: 16 hours of mediated/home study and 4 hours live, including two pharmacy-law hours. All sessions are approved, but nine CE hours were earned on one single calendar day; remaining hours were on compliant days. Does this satisfy the 2026 minimum?

choices.text: Yes, because the pharmacist earned 20 approved hours and at least two were pharmacy law.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule separately caps home study at 15 hours toward the annual minimum and credits no more than eight hours in one day.

choices.text: No; only 15 mediated plus four live CE hours may count, leaving fewer than 20 hours for the year.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 4.03(4)(b) limits mediated credits, and §4.03(7) adds an independent daily limit.

choices.text: Yes, because legal-education credits override the annual limits on mediated instruction.
choices.why: Incorrect. Pharmacy-law subject compliance does not exempt other format and daily requirements.

choices.text: No, but uncounted extra hours automatically carry into 2027 and cure the 2026 deficit.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 4.03(5) prohibits carrying CE from one calendar year into another.

items.novelty_note: Combines daily/mediated limits rather than repeating old biennial aggregate.

items.stem: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist is ARRESTED in another state on November 2. Criminal charges remain pending. On November 10, an unrelated professional licensing board imposes a disciplinary restriction. No conviction has occurred. Which obligations arise under 247 CMR 20.03? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Report the arrest to the Massachusetts Board within 14 calendar days, even before any conviction.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 20.03(3) explicitly includes arrest and pending charges.

choices.text: Wait for conviction before any criminal-history report, because an arrest is not a final finding.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Massachusetts Board reporting requirement is triggered earlier than conviction.

choices.text: Report the other licensing board's professional disciplinary restriction within 14 calendar days.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 20.03(4) independently covers disciplinary action and loss of certification.

choices.text: Reporting both matters to the pharmacist's employer satisfies the Massachusetts Board requirements.
choices.why: Incorrect. Employment records are not a substitute for the specified Board reports.

items.novelty_note: Two separate triggers in one professional history; no wait for conviction.

items.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy has three people scheduled to perform pharmacist duties. One holds a current unrestricted Massachusetts pharmacist registration. Another is licensed but subject to a current Board order prohibiting controlled-substance handling. The third pharmacist's registration expired yesterday and renewal is pending. Who can be assigned final validation for a Schedule II prescription, assuming all normal reviews are performed?

choices.text: The pharmacist with an active, unrestricted Massachusetts license, who completes all required reviews.
choices.why: Correct. This pharmacist has the necessary current authority, subject to performing all required checks.

choices.text: The pharmacist whose renewal is pending, because filing a renewal preserves authority automatically.
choices.why: Incorrect. A pending application is not an active license.

choices.text: The pharmacist whose Board order prohibits controlled substances, because validation is not the same as selecting tablets.
choices.why: Incorrect. Validating a Schedule II prescription would violate the current practice restriction.

choices.text: A nationally certified technician, if a pharmacist approves a batch report later.
choices.why: Incorrect. Final prescription validation is a pharmacist duty and cannot be delegated to technicians.

items.novelty_note: Operational restriction/expired license comparison, not impairment-program timing.
